tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Classify a causal LTI system as BIBO stable or unstable by checking whether every transfer-function pole lies strictly in the left half of the s-plane.

sections.section_title: Introduction to BIBO Stability from Pole Locations

blocks.text: From the prior lesson, the prerequisite for this topic is already established: the system must be causal before applying pole-based BIBO tests. The object to track in this step is a transfer function written in the rational form $H(s)=\frac{N(s)}{D(s)}$.

Next define the poles as the roots of the denominator polynomial: if $D(s)=\prod_i (s-p_i)$, then each $p_i$ is a pole location in the complex $s$-plane. The left half-plane is the set of points where $\Re\{s\}<0$.

For a causal LTI system, the direct rule is strict: BIBO stability is true exactly when every pole has negative real part. This means $\Re\{p_i\}<0$ for each pole $p_i$ and any pole with $\Re\{p_i\}\ge 0$ is not allowed in this check.

blocks.latex: \text{BIBO stable for causal LTI} \iff \Re\{p_i\}<0\;\text{for every pole }p_i.

blocks.text: Use the base case $H(s)=\frac{1}{s+2}$. The denominator is $s+2$, so the only pole is $-2$. Since $\Re\{-2\}=-2<0$, this transfer function is BIBO stable.

Contrast examples by inspection: $H(s)=\frac{1}{s-1}$ has pole $p=1$, so $\Re\{p\}>0$ and it is unstable. $H(s)=\frac{1}{s}$ has pole on the imaginary axis, $\Re\{p\}=0$, so it is not accepted as BIBO stable under this strict criterion.

Use this same move in three representations: listed poles, factored transfer functions, and pole-zero style lists. In later sections, the action stays the same: check causality first, then apply the pole sign test to classify each system as BIBO stable or unstable.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Causal LTI System from Listed Pole Locations

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is the explicit pole list $\{p_1,p_2,p_3\}$. For a causal LTI system, apply the strict BIBO rule: every pole must be in the left half-plane, so each pole must satisfy $\Re\{p_i\}<0$.
Execute the test pole-by-pole. The three real parts are $\Re\{p_1\}=-1$, $\Re\{p_2\}=-3$, and $\Re\{p_3\}=2$.
Check the strict inequality: $p_1$ and $p_2$ satisfy $\Re\{p_i\}<0$, but $p_3=2$ does not because its real part is positive. A single violating pole is sufficient to fail the criterion.
So this example is not BIBO stable because of the pole at $2$, and the result is unstable for the causal LTI system.

sections.section_title: Classifying Stability from a Factored Transfer Function

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a transfer function written with factored denominator factors. Use the BIBO stability cue: for a causal LTI system, all poles must be strictly in the left half-plane, so the rule is $\Re(p)<0$ for every pole.
Start by extracting poles from the denominator only. Set each denominator factor to zero: $(s+1)=0$, $(s+3)=0$, and $(s+6)=0$. This gives poles $p_1=-1$, $p_2=-3$, and $p_3=-6$.
Check each real part: $\Re(p_1)=-1$, $\Re(p_2)=-3$, and $\Re(p_3)=-6$. Every pole satisfies the strict left-half-plane condition.
Since all poles are strictly negative on the real axis, the system is BIBO stable.

sections.section_title: Classifying Stability from a Pole-Zero Plot

image_slots.image_description: Create an s-plane pole-zero plot with horizontal real axis labeled Re(s), vertical imaginary axis labeled Im(s), and clear coordinate grid. Show poles at $s=-1$, $s=-4$, and $s=0.8$ as pole markers, and zeros at $s=+2j$ and $s=-2j$ as zero markers. Keep axes and markers legible, with each marker visually coded by type (x for poles, o for zeros) and an unobtrusive note that stability depends on pole real parts only.

example_content.example_prompt: Use the provided pole-zero plot to classify stability for poles at $-1$, $-4$, and $0.8$ with zeros at $\pm j2$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is an s-plane pole-zero plot. Your action is to read the pole locations, then apply the same strict rule from earlier sections: a causal LTI system is BIBO stable only if every pole satisfies $\Re(p)<0$.
First, extract the poles from the plot: $-1$, $-4$, and $0.8$. Ignore zero locations at this step, because zeros do not enter the BIBO pole test.
Next, compute the real parts of the poles: $\Re(-1)=-1$, $\Re(-4)=-4$, and $\Re(0.8)=0.8$. Check each one against the strict condition $\Re(p)<0$.
Because $0.8$ is in the right half-plane, the rule fails, so the system is not BIBO stable. The result is unstable.

sections.section_title: Detecting Instability from One Pole Outside the Strict Left Half-Plane

explanation_blocks.text: This is the pole-sign diagnostic form: extract all poles from the transfer function denominator, then apply the same strict left-half-plane rule as before.
Set each denominator factor to zero: $(s+3)=0$, $(s+0.5)=0$, and $(s-0.1)=0$, so the poles are $p_1=-3$, $p_2=-0.5$, and $p_3=0.1$.
The outlier is $0.1$, which lies in the right half-plane. Because one pole violates the strict condition, the system is unstable.

question_entry.lesson_core_move: Classify a causal LTI system as BIBO stable or unstable by checking whether every transfer-function pole lies strictly in the left half of the s-plane.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Causal LTI System from Listed Pole Locations

prompt_blocks.text: A causal LTI system has transfer-function poles $p=\{-1,-2,-4\}$. Which statement correctly applies the BIBO pole test?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because every pole satisfies $\Re\{p_i\}<0$.
BIBO unstable, because at least one pole has negative real part.
BIBO unstable, because stability depends on pole magnitude $|p_i|$ rather than real part sign.
BIBO stable, because zeros, not poles, determine the stability test.
BIBO unstable, because the pole $p=-4$ is farthest from the origin.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable, because all listed poles satisfy $\Re\{p_i\}<0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For a causal LTI system, BIBO stability requires every transfer-function pole to lie strictly in the left half-plane. The poles $-1$, $-2$, and $-4$ all have negative real parts, so the system is BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: A causal LTI system has transfer-function poles $p=\{-3,-1+j2,-1-j2,0\}$. Which statement correctly applies the BIBO pole test?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because no pole has positive real part.
BIBO unstable, because the pole at $0$ does not satisfy $\Re\{p_i\}<0$.
BIBO stable, because the complex poles have negative real parts and their imaginary parts do not matter.
BIBO unstable, because the complex poles have nonzero imaginary parts.
BIBO stable, because the pole magnitudes are finite.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO unstable, because one pole is at $0$, so not every pole has $\Re\{p_i\}<0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The strict causal BIBO stability test is that every pole must have negative real part. The poles $-3$ and $-1\pm j2$ satisfy the test, but the pole at $0$ has real part $0$, not a negative real part. Therefore the system is BIBO unstable.

sections.section_title: Classifying Stability from a Factored Transfer Function

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the BIBO stability of $H(s)=\dfrac{3(s+1)}{(s+1)(s+4)(s+5)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because the denominator poles are $-1$, $-4$, and $-5$.
BIBO unstable, because the numerator zero at $s=-1$ appears in the denominator.
BIBO unstable, because the pole from $(s+1)$ is $s=1$.
Not BIBO stable, because strict stability requires every pole to satisfy $\Re(p)>0$.
BIBO stable, because the numerator has a zero at $s=-1$.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable, because the denominator poles are $-1$, $-4$, and $-5$, and each satisfies $\Re(p)<0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For BIBO stability of a causal LTI system, inspect the denominator factors. The factors $(s+1)$, $(s+4)$, and $(s+5)$ give poles $-1$, $-4$, and $-5$.
All three poles are strictly in the left half-plane, so the system is BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the BIBO stability of $H(s)=\dfrac{5(s+2)}{(s+3)(s-1)(s+7)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because the numerator zero is at $s=-2$.
BIBO unstable, because one denominator pole is $s=1$.
BIBO stable, because the denominator poles have finite magnitudes $1$, $3$, and $7$.
BIBO stable, because two denominator poles are negative.
Not enough information, because BIBO stability cannot be classified from denominator factors.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO unstable, because the denominator factor $(s-1)$ gives the pole $s=1$, which has $\Re(p)>0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the denominator factors to find the poles. The factors $(s+3)$, $(s-1)$, and $(s+7)$ give poles $-3$, $1$, and $-7$.
Because the pole $s=1$ is in the right half-plane, not every pole satisfies $\Re(p)<0$. The causal system is therefore BIBO unstable.

sections.section_title: Classifying Stability from a Pole-Zero Plot

image_slots.image_description: Create an s-plane pole-zero plot with horizontal real axis labeled Re(s) and vertical imaginary axis labeled Im(s). Show pole markers (x) at $s=-3$, $s=-0$.5+1.5j, and $s=-0$.5-1.5j. Show zero markers (o) at $s=1$.5 and $s=-2j$. Use a coordinate grid and lightly shade or label the left half-plane and right half-plane; keep a small note that BIBO stability depends only on pole real parts.

Create an s-plane pole-zero plot with horizontal real axis labeled Re(s) and vertical imaginary axis labeled Im(s). Show pole markers (x) at $s=-2$, $s=-1-j1$, and $s=+j1 on the imaginary axis$. Show zero markers (o) at $s=-3 and s=2$. Use a coordinate grid and lightly shade or label the left half-plane and right half-plane; make the imaginary-axis pole visually clear because the strict left-half-plane test is the key.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the pole-zero plot for a causal LTI system. Which option correctly classifies BIBO stability?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable; all plotted poles have $\Re(p)<0$.
BIBO unstable; the zero at $s=1.5$ is in the right half-plane.
BIBO unstable; the pole closest to the imaginary axis controls by distance only.
BIBO stable; zeros cancel the pole-location test.
BIBO unstable; stability requires every zero to be in the left half-plane.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable because every pole is strictly in the left half-plane.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The poles are at $-3$ and $-0.5\pm j1.5$, so every pole has negative real part. The right-half-plane zero does not affect the causal BIBO pole test, so the system is BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the pole-zero plot for a causal LTI system. Which option correctly classifies BIBO stability?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable; no pole is strictly in the right half-plane.
BIBO unstable; the pole on the imaginary axis is not strictly in the left half-plane.
BIBO stable; the left-half-plane zero makes the system stable.
BIBO unstable; the right-half-plane zero determines the classification.
BIBO stable; poles on the imaginary axis satisfy $\Re(p)<0$.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO unstable because one pole lies on the imaginary axis.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pole at $j1$ has real part $0$, not a strictly negative real part. Since causal BIBO stability requires every pole to satisfy $\Re(p)<0$, the system is BIBO unstable even though no pole is to the right of the imaginary axis.

sections.section_title: Detecting Instability from One Pole Outside the Strict Left Half-Plane

choice_blocks.text: Stable because two of the three poles are in the left half-plane.
Unstable because the pole at $s=2$ is in the right half-plane.
Stable because the stability test uses $\Re(p)\le 0$ for every pole.
Stable because the numerator has no finite zeros.
Unstable only if the right-half-plane pole is repeated.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable because the denominator has a pole at $s=2$, and $\Re(2)>0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator factors give poles $-1$, $-4$, and $2$. BIBO stability for this causal LTI system requires every pole to satisfy $\Re(p)<0$. Since $2$ is in the right half-plane, one pole violates the strict condition, so the system is unstable.

choice_blocks.text: Stable because the pole at $s=0$ satisfies $\Re(p)\le 0$.
Unstable because the pole at $s=0$ is not strictly in the left half-plane.
Stable because the two negative poles dominate the pole at the origin.
Stable because only zeros, not poles, determine BIBO stability.
Unstable only if there are more nonnegative poles than negative poles.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable because the pole at $s=0$ has $\Re(0)=0$, which is outside the strict left half-plane.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator gives poles $0$, $-2$, and $-6$. The strict criterion is $\Re(p)<0$ for every pole. The pole at $0$ lies on the imaginary axis rather than in the strict left half-plane, so the system is not BIBO stable.
